cards.title: In hindsight
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This is a critical analysis of current constitutional developments and Pakistan's international legal obligations.
cards.summary: A report by the International Commission of Jurists argues that the 26th and 27th Amendments have compromised judicial independence in Pakistan. The report suggests these constitutional changes have placed the higher courts under executive and political influence. Consequently, Pakistan may be failing to meet international standards regarding the right to an effective legal remedy.
key_facts: The ICJ report is titled Judicial Capture: Independence of the Judiciary in Pakistan after the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments.
The ICJ states that these amendments risk violating Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
The report claims that loss of judicial independence affects the right to an effective legal remedy under Article 2(3) of the ICCPR.
The ICJ includes judges and lawyers dedicated to strengthening global justice systems.

vocab.meaning: Great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause.
Formal safeguards that protect an organization's autonomy.

text: JUST as an important partner in the ruling coalition is starting to question the wisdom of the 26th and 27th Amendments, a report issued by the International Commission of Jurists has detailed the damage the two enactments have wrought on Pakistan’s judiciary.

Titled Judicial Capture: Independence of the Judiciary in Pakistan after the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments, the report concludes that systemic constitutional and legislative changes have placed the country’s highest courts under the control of the political and executive branches.

The ICJ comprises judges and lawyers from around the world working to “develop and strengthen national and international justice systems”. The report clarifies: “The ICJ does not take a position on the merits of political disputes between the parties. Its analysis is focused on the institutional framework in which the judiciary operates, and whether it is consistent with Pakistan’s obligations under international law.”

The most worrying flag the report raises is that the ruling parties — in what can only be read as their zeal to have these two amendments enacted — have pushed the judiciary to a state where the country’s highest courts no longer “enjoy the institutional guarantees of independence required by Article 14” of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the UN Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, among other standards.
It also notes that the loss of judicial independence has stripped victims of human rights abuses of their right to an effective legal remedy under domestic law and Article 2(3) of the ICCPR.

Though the ICJ agrees that prior issues in the Pakistani judiciary, especially its tendency to overreach into parliament’s domain, needed targeted reforms, its secretary-general, Santiago Canton, says the government used those frustrations as a pretext to seize full control of the judiciary rather than enact serious reforms.

The detailed report offers a cold examination of the path taken by the Pakistani judiciary since 2024 and brings into fresh relief what may be the roots of some of the new crises that have gripped the country since then. Its timing couldn’t have been better: there is speculation that another amendment is in the works, and those who partnered with the government on getting earlier legislation enacted are now apprehensive of what a new rewrite will entail.

As local observers have been warning, and as the ICJ’s findings now bear out, the 26th and 27th Amendments have done serious damage to judicial independence. Part of the reason why is the haste with which they were enacted. Before any further changes are made to the Constitution, it would be wise to debate all proposed amendments at length and enact them only after a careful, deliberate consensus has been built.

cards.title: Childhoods forsaken
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This covers essential social issues including education, child rights, and public health, which are common themes in competitive exams.
cards.summary: World Children’s Day highlights the systemic failure to protect Pakistan's youth from violence, neglect, and exploitation. Statistics reveal high rates of child abuse and significant barriers to education and health. While some legislative progress exists regarding marriage age, enforcement and oversight remain the primary obstacles to safeguarding children.
key_facts: Sahil recorded 1,914 child abuse cases in the first half of 2026, including 558 abductions.
Unicef estimates 25.1 million children aged five to 16 are out of school in Pakistan.
A study suggests 1.5 million internet-using children in Pakistan experienced online sexual abuse in one year.
Nine polio cases were reported in Pakistan by early November 2026.

vocab.meaning: Lack of proper nutrition due to poor diet or health issues.

text: WORLD Children’s Day, observed today, should be a celebration of childhood. In Pakistan, it is a reminder of how often children are denied even basic safety. At least 28 schoolchildren died when a roof collapsed in Peshawar last month; in August, a fire at Islamabad’s Pims hospital killed 14 newborns. Both tragedies raise serious questions about safety standards in schools and hospitals. Reports of children raped and murdered, sometimes by people they knew, point to dangers closer to home. Sahil documented 1,914 child abuse cases in the first half of 2026, including 1,015 cases of sexual abuse and 558 abductions. These were only cases reported in newspapers; the true scale of abuse is likely far greater. Children also face exploitation online. A Unicef-backed study estimated that 1.5m internet-using children aged 12 to 17 experienced technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse in a year. Yet despite the scale of these dangers, effective protection remains out of reach.

Violence and abuse are only part of the hardship confronting Pakistan’s children. Unicef estimates that 25.1m children aged five to 16 are out of school. Malnutrition and preventable disease remain widespread, while nine polio cases had been reported by early November. Child marriage continues to interrupt girls’ education and expose them to early motherhood. There has been some progress. Punjab joined Sindh, Balochistan and Islamabad this year in setting 18 as the minimum marriage age, though KP has yet to follow suit. The Benazir Nashonuma Programme has also been extended to support more vulnerable women and children. But laws need enforcement, and schemes need sustained funding and oversight, particularly in areas where public services are weakest. School and hospital safety inspections, effective investigations of abuse, support for survivors and stronger safeguards online are essential. Birth registration, vaccination, nutrition and access to schooling also demand attention. Officials must be held accountable for disasters, and investigations must lead to action. Pakistan cannot keep failing its children and then celebrating them once a year. The real disgrace is not that these failures are unknown, but that they are allowed to continue.

cards.title: Settling disputes
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: This is relevant for understanding judicial reforms and the challenges of alternative dispute resolution in Pakistan's legal system.
cards.summary: Punjab is considering a panchayat system to help manage the nearly two million pending court cases. While community-based dispute resolution can offer relief, the government must learn from previous failed attempts and experiences in other countries. The aim is to create a more accessible justice system, but small, well-regulated steps are necessary for success.
key_facts: There are nearly 2 million court cases pending in the lower judiciary, mostly in Punjab.
The Punjab Alternative Dispute Resolution Act, 2019 was recently repealed by an ordinance in 2026.
The proposed panchayat system aims to resolve local-level disputes through community decision-making.
Legal scholars suggest studying India's village justice court system to understand potential outcomes.

vocab.meaning: Temporary breaks or postponements of court proceedings.
A village council or traditional local assembly.
